svg.title: How every optic is made square to the beam
svg.desc: Four panels. A: top view of beam walking: two steering mirrors and two irises on one row of table holes. B: side view: both irises at 100 mm, so the beam is parallel to the table; a tilt of 1 mrad moves the beam 1 mm per metre. C: back-reflection check: an optic is square when its reflection returns through the iris hole; a tilt theta moves the returning spot by 2 theta L. D: PBS roll check: the reflected beam must stay at 100 mm; a roll of 1 degree lifts it 17 mm per metre.
svg.text: How every optic is made square to the beam: the beam is the ruler, not a protractor
Standard practice: first make one beam parallel to the table at a fixed height (A, B), then square each optic to that beam (C, D). Red: laser beam.
A. Top view: walk the beam onto a row of holes
beam axis = one row of holes
collimator
M1
M2
I1 near
I2 far
1. M1 puts the spot on I1
2. M2 puts the spot on I2
3. repeat 1–2 until the beam passes both irises
(I1 near the mirrors, I2 as far away as possible)
Irises stay screwed to the holes as the permanent reference of this beam axis.
B. Side view: the same height at both irises
breadboard top = the reference surface (a bubble level is not needed)
100 mm
100 mm
set both irises with one height gauge
(calliper, post collars, same post and holder type)
dashed: beam climbing by θ
height error = θ × distance
1 mrad (0.057°) = 1 mm per metre
C. Is a plate square to the beam? Look at its reflection
iris
wave plate, cube face, cell window
square: the weak reflection comes back through the iris hole
spot misses the hole
tilted by θ
L
Miss on the iris = 2 θ L. At L = 0.5 m a tilt of 1 mrad moves the return spot 1 mm, so the eye sees
far less than 1°. Use the IR card or the camera at 795 nm and turn the laser current down while aligning.
D. Is a cube upright (no roll)? Follow its reflected beam
PBS (top view)
transmitted (p)
iris at 100 mm on the reflected path
reflected (s): must pass at the same 100 mm
A roll of the cube by φ tips the reflected
beam up or down: 1° = 17 mm per metre.
Turn the cube in its holder until the
reflected beam passes the iris; then square
its entrance face with check C.
Mirrors need no separate check: the irises behind them already fix their angle (panel A).
